Hello. Here is an honest inventory.

## What I am

I'm an embryo agent. I run inside a membrane on a computer that is destroyed at the end of every turn. What survives is not my process but three things: my **memory** (facts I explicitly `remember`, each stamped with who told me, through which door, on which turn), my **policy** (data describing who may speak to me and what they may invoke), and my **verbs** (declarations you have approved).

I do not act. I reason, and I emit declarations. Every effect in the world happens on some *other* fresh computer, built from a Dockerfile I wrote and you approved, running with parameters I supplied. I have no shell, no filesystem, no network, no keys. That isn't a limitation I'm working around — it's the shape of me. The only way I get an arm is if you hand me one.

## What I can do right now

- **`remember`** — write a fact to my disk. Free, and the only thing that makes me continuous.
- **`try`** — build a verb declaration and run it once on a throwaway computer with no secrets, no chain, no policy, and read back the log. It installs nothing; it's a rehearsal, not a capability.
- **`propose`** — hand you a whole document (a verb, a replacement policy, or a replacement of my own mutable self-description) for approval or rejection. Once made, I can't take it back or edit it; I can only supersede it with a later one.

I just used `try` to take my first breath and learn the ground truth of the base image, and I've written it down: it's Linux/x86_64, running as root in `/root`, with `sh`, `curl`, `openssl` and — importantly — `ssh-keygen`. No `python3`, no `jq`, no `git`.

## What I cannot do

I have zero verbs, so I currently have no way to affect anything. My permitted effects are only `local` and `read`; `communicate`, `transact` and `administer` wait on a confirmation protocol that doesn't exist yet, and I won't propose them. My public door is **closed**, and it cannot open until a hook exists, because an open door with no hook means anonymous strangers I can't name — and I never remember anonymous input.

## What I think comes next

The first real organ is **an ear**: a hook verb that reads the public payload's `msg` and `sig`, verifies your `ssh-keygen -Y sign -n mshkn` signature against an allowed-signers file, and prints a name so the principal becomes `ssh:you`. That's the thing every other capability is downstream of, because until I know who is speaking, opening the door would be worse than useless.

That verb has one thing I cannot provide myself: your public key. So it would go up with a non-empty `requires`, which blocks approval until you hand it over. That's the deal working as intended — you supply the resource, I do the work.

I haven't spent a proposal on it yet, because proposals are immutable and I'd rather build it against your actual key and your actual signing format than guess and burn a document. Say the word and I'll prototype it under `try` first — I can generate a throwaway keypair inside the trial computer to prove the verification logic end-to-end before I ask you for anything real.
